source: Energy of a System of Charges
Add kqᵢqⱼ/rᵢⱼ over every pair to find the energy needed to assemble the charges.
Students count each pair twice, or leave some pairs out.

Two charges store potential energy $U = kq_1q_2/r$: positive if they repel, negative if they attract. What about three charges, or a dozen? The energy of the whole group is the work it takes to assemble it, bringing the charges in from far away one at a time.

$$U = \sum_{\text{pairs } i < j}\frac{kq_iq_j}{r_{ij}}$$
        One term for each pair, counted once. $N$ charges make $N(N-1)/2$ pairs.

Assemble the charges one at a time. The first costs nothing: no other charges are there yet. The second costs $kq_1q_2/r_{12}$. The third moves through the potential of the first two, costing $q_3(V_1 + V_2) = kq_1q_3/r_{13} + kq_2q_3/r_{23}$. Each new charge adds one term for each charge already present, so in the end every pair appears exactly once. The order of assembly does not matter; the total is the same.
Three charges, three pairs. Drag them: pulling the attracting pair apart takes work, pushing the repelling pairs together takes work too.

This energy belongs to the arrangement as a whole, not to any one charge. Its sign tells a story. Positive $U$ means repulsion won while you built the group: let go, and the charges fly apart, turning $U$ into kinetic energy. Negative $U$ means attraction won: the group is bound, and you must supply $|U|$ to take it apart. The same bookkeeping explains why atoms and ionic crystals hold together.
Worked examples
Charges of $+3.0$, $-2.0$ and $+1.0\ \mu\text{C}$ sit in a line, $0.10\ \text{m}$ apart in that order. Find $U$.
Three in a line
$U \approx -0.584\ \text{J}$
$U = -0.584\ \text{J}$. Negative: assembling them released energy, and pulling them apart would take that much work.
Four $2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ charges sit at the corners of a square with $0.10\ \text{m}$ sides. Find $U$.
Four at the corners of a square
$U \approx 1.95\ \text{J}$
$4 \cdot 3/2 = 6$ pairs: four along the sides ($r = a$) and two across the diagonals ($r = a\sqrt{2}$).
How much work does it take to bring a fifth charge, $+1.0\ \mu\text{C}$, from far away to the center of that square?
Adding one more
$W \approx 1.02\ \text{J}$
The work for the newcomer is its charge times the potential the others make there: $W = qV$. The energy among the first four does not change.
Each corner is $a/\sqrt{2} = 0.0707\ \text{m}$ from the center: $V = 4\cdot\dfrac{kq}{a/\sqrt{2}} = 1.02 \times 10^{6}\ \text{V}$.

Counting each pair twice, or skipping some. Summing $kq_iq_j/r_{ij}$ over every $i$ and every $j \ne i$ counts each pair twice and doubles $U$. Forgetting the diagonals of a square leaves pairs out. Check the number of terms: it must be $N(N-1)/2$, so 3 for three charges and 6 for four.
